It is played in every county of Ireland, with its core in the mid-west. Early makers include the English flautist Charles Nicholson II; in the later nineteenth century the London firms Rudall & Rose and Boosey brought out large-hole Pratten flutes. The Belfast-born flute maker Samuel Colin Hamilton argues that the military flute and fife bands common in nineteenth-century Ireland made society familiar with the flute as a dance instrument, and that the economic improvement of the mid-nineteenth century let more people obtain instruments. Modern makers mostly copy the old patterns, adjusting the tuning to suit traditional music.

Traditional music often plays it in unison in the keys of D, G or A major; the technique is close to that of the whistle, using cuts, strikes and rolls as ornament, some of them taken from the Irish bagpipe tradition. The military flute and fife bands of nineteenth-century Ireland also helped the flute into dance music settings.

The Irish flute is an aerophone, classification number 421.121.12: a conical-bore, simple-system wooden transverse flute, usually played with six main finger holes opened and closed to give the major scale, with some instruments adding metal keys or a seventh hole for the little finger to obtain semitones. It descends from the pattern used by classical flute players in the early nineteenth century, and the modern version is mostly adjusted for Irish traditional music, Scottish traditional music, Breton music and other Celtic national musics, and is also found in dance music. The player blows across the flute, controlling the mouth hole together with the fingering; most Irish traditional players use a wooden six-hole flute. It is used in every county of Ireland, concentrated in the mid-western areas of Roscommon, Leitrim, Sligo, south Fermanagh, east Galway, Clare and west Limerick.
愛爾蘭長笛為氣鳴樂器，採圓錐管、簡單系統六孔指法。以 D 調為例，六孔全閉至全開: The Irish flute is an aerophone with a conical bore and simple-system six-hole fingering. In D, for example, closing all six holes and opening them in turn gives the D major scale, and the D an octave above can be overblown. The wooden body, the characteristic embouchure and the direct fingering make its timbre different from the Western concert flute, often breathier; Irish players mostly aim for a darker tone with a hint of reediness. Volume depends on the bore design: the large-bore Pratten style gives more volume, while the Rudall & Rose style is a little thinner in tone. Compared with the Boehm-system metal flute, the sound is still produced by opening and closing finger holes.
愛爾蘭長笛琴身以木製為主，傳統常見材質包括可卡斯木、格瑞那迪拉（非洲黑木）、玫瑰: The body of the Irish flute is mostly wood, traditionally including cocuswood, grenadilla (African blackwood), rosewood, ebony and boxwood. Modern instruments are also made of Delrin, PVC or bamboo, but wood is still the most common. The source does not state the material of the sounding body. The added keys of older flutes use pewter plugs and silver pads; modern versions may be keyless or carry varying numbers of metal keys.
